changes.before: Remove editable.add(3). What does view.size show?
changes.after: A read-only list view can still see changes made through another name.

before: List<Int> describes a list of Int values and exposes read operations. It does not necessarily prove the underlying collection cannot change through another reference.
mutableListOf creates a mutable list. Assigning it to a List<Int> view does not copy its elements.
Adding through the mutable reference changes the same list seen through its read-only view.
val prevents rebinding the variable, not changes supported by the referenced object.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin
fun main() {
    val editable = mutableListOf(1, 2)
    val view: List<Int> = editable
    editable.add(3)
    println(view.size)
}

```
Expected output or behavior: 3. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare a read-only view with a copied list. Explain what changes when another reference mutates the source. You may trace it without a Kotlin compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A list keeps items in order. A mutable list lets you add, remove, or replace items. The function `mutableListOf` creates one.
`List<Int>` means a list view of Int values. This type lets you read items, but it does not provide the functions for changing the list.
Assigning editable to view does not copy the list. Both names refer to the same list, with different allowed actions.
Using `val` keeps each name linked to its assigned value. It does not freeze the contents of a mutable list.

Follow the example one line at a time.
```kotlin
fun main() {
    val editable = mutableListOf(1, 2)
    val view: List<Int> = editable
    editable.add(3)
    println(view.size)
}

```
The screen shows `3`. Adding through editable changes the shared list, so view sees three items too.
Read-only describes what you may do through one reference. It does not promise that nobody else can change the same list.

before.question: Remove editable.add(3). What does view.size show?
choices: 2 because both references still view the original two elements.
3 because a read-only view always copies a third element.
before.explanation: The view shares the same collection; without the addition there are only two elements.

after.question: Remove `editable.add(3)`. What does view.size show?
choices: 2, because the shared list still has its original two items.
3, because a read-only view adds an item.
0, because List cannot refer to a mutable list.
after.explanation: No item is added. Both names still refer to the list containing 1 and 2, so its size is 2.
